name: BoolQ
description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer ('yes' or 'no'). The dataset contains 16,000 questions split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set. Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and paired with Wikipedia passages by human annotators.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
publisher: Google AI Language / University of Washington
citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions.
rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. The question and Wikipedia page are then given to a human annotator for further processing. 13k questions were gathered from this pipeline and combined with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer are used.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine paired with Wikipedia pages returned as one of the first five search results. Additionally, 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set were included.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. Queries are heuristically filtered to identify yes/no questions by selecting those where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words ('did', 'do', 'does', 'is', 'are', 'was', 'were', 'have', 'has', 'can', 'could', 'will', 'would') and are of sufficient length. Each question is paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document to reduce ambiguity and keep input size manageable.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions from NQ are always placed in the train set. The 16k questions are split into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set. Each question is paired with the annotator-selected passage rather than the full Wikipedia document.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) they decide if the question is 'good' (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page; (2) for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, and can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information; (3) annotators mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'. Annotation quality was assessed by having three of the authors label 110 randomly chosen examples, conferring on disagreements to select a single answer by mutual agreement, resulting in 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Singly-annotated examples are used in the training/dev/test sets.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. Disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to produce gold-standard labels. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where annotations differed from gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Since agreement was sufficiently high, singly-annotated examples were used to allow gathering a larger dataset.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 (singly-annotated examples used in training/dev/test sets; 110 examples were labeled by 3 authors for quality assessment)
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has been noted to have been updated at least once since initial analysis (footnote 4 mentions the dataset has been updated since the inference type analysis was carried out). Data and code are available at https://goo.gl/boolq.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions, which has real-world applications in question answering systems. The questions are naturally occurring, meaning they reflect genuine information needs of users.
rai:dataBiases: 'Yes' answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set), creating a class imbalance. There is a correlation between the nature/topic of the question and the likelihood of a 'yes' answer, though this correlation is too weak to outperform the majority baseline.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is class imbalanced with 62.31% 'yes' answers. The inference type analysis may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset has been updated since that analysis was carried out. The dataset uses singly-annotated examples, which may introduce some annotation noise (estimated ~10% error rate). The best model achieves only 80.4% accuracy compared to 90% human accuracy, leaving a significant gap.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, development (validation), and testing of reading comprehension and yes/no question answering models. The dataset is intended to test models' ability to make complex inferences from text, including entailment-like reasoning. It can also be used as a fine-tuning target for transfer learning experiments.
